body.text: In short:
Archaeologists have unearthed teeth belonging to an ancient human known as Homo erectus in mainland China.
The discovery indicates that it lived in the region much longer than previously thought and provides the first evidence that it could survive in rainforests.
Another tooth found from an unidentified hominin indicates H. erectus may have interacted with other human species.
Troves of fossilised teeth collected by ancient Chinese porcupines in two caves show that Homo sapiens were not the only human species to adapt to rainforests.
Trace chemical elements in the teeth of Homo erectus and a bevy of forest animals have helped scientists fill in gaps about when the ancient hominin lived in the region and how it survived.

Two studies in the journal Nature — from Australian, Chinese and European researchers — identified Homo erectus teeth dated between 324,000 and 184,000 years old in southern China and reconstructed the ancient ecosystems this species called home.
The discovery means Homo erectus lived in mainland Asia longer than thought, and challenges assumptions that they did not have the skills to live in rainforests.
Homo erectus were an ancient ancestor of modern humans that lived from 2 million to 108,000 years ago. They migrated from the cradle of Africa out to Europe and Asia about 1.8 million years ago.
Until now, the youngest Homo erectus fossil in China was about 400,000 years old.

Kira Westaway, a geo-chronologist from Macquarie University, said it had previously been thought that Homo erectus went extinct as their preferred landscapes, grassland savannas and open woodlands, changed into rainforests.
"But this assumption has been challenged by our new Homo erectus evidence from two neighbouring caves in southern China," Professor Westaway said.
"They give evidence of Homo erectus surviving in rainforests."
The studies indicate the species may have not just survived in rainforests but also travelled great distances instead of staying in a single location.
How the teeth were found
Nine hominin teeth were found across two caves, Baxian and Naxian, about 20 kilometres north of the city of Chongzuo in China's south.
Eight of the teeth were linked to Homo erectus, while the ninth tooth was from another unidentified species of ancient human.
Scientists also discovered fossils from a range of animals including elephants, bears, canines, pigs, rhinos and monkeys.

Study co-author palaeontologist Yingqi Zhang, from the Institute of Vertebrate Palaeontology and Palaeoanthropology at the Chinese Academy of Sciences, said the two fossil deposits contained some bone fragments but were mainly teeth.
He said the teeth, which were in sediment estimated to be 324,000 to 184,000 years old, were likely gathered by ancient porcupines.
"Porcupines have this kind of habit [where] they collect bones and gnaw them to sharpen their incisors," Professor Zhang said.
"These teeth we found in a cave are the things they [porcupines] left behind because teeth are the hardest tissue in our body."
What was in the teeth?
Several tests, including the analysis of the metal strontium, which is found in the enamel of teeth, were used to figure out what Homo erectus and the other animals ate.
Study author and geo-chronologist Renaud Joannes-Boyau, from Southern Cross University, said it appeared Homo erectus was living in a dense rainforest at the top of the food chain.
To find out how Homo erectus survived, the researchers cut into the tooth enamel to see bands of growth and figure out what the hominin ate at different stages of life and where.
And it appeared that, at an early point in life, these ancient hominins ate food about 250km away in what is now Vietnam.
"They're very flexible, they're adaptable, and they're mobile, which I think is something that we believe was only [possible] for Homo sapiens," Professor Joannes-Boyau said.
Griffith University palaeontologist Julien Louys, who was not involved in the study, said the research represented the first evidence that Homo erectus lived in rainforest environments.

"While the sample size for this conclusion is small, if substantiated it would suggest a degree of ecological flexibility unmatched in the hominin lineage until the later arrival of Denisovans and modern humans."

La Trobe University archaeologist Jesse Martin, who was not involved in the study, said it was not shocking that the species was able to survive in rainforest environments, as it lasted in Indonesia until about 100,000 years ago.
"Indeed, this study reinforces the fact that Homo erectus continued to survive in rainforest environments long after the species had gone extinct elsewhere."
What happened to Homo erectus?
There is still plenty of mystery surrounding why Homo erectus became extinct.
Professor Joannes-Boyau said the next big question to answer was how the species may have interacted with other hominins.

The researchers speculated the mystery ninth tooth could have belonged to a Denisovan (Homo longi), a type of human that appears in the fossil record from about 200,000 years ago in China, or a new species altogether.
The oldest Homo sapiens teeth in the country have been dated between 120,000 and 80,000 years old.
Professor Louys said the studies suggested the three species almost overlapped in time.
"Certainly they are found much closer in time than previously demonstrated," he said.
"Overall, it really highlights how little we know about hominin evolution in this part of the world.
"The studies raise a whole bunch more questions about the uniqueness of our own species."
Dr Martin said Homo erectus likely encountered Denisovans, Neanderthals, and us towards the end of their global domination as a species.
As a result, he said, increased competition for resources may ultimately have driven the species extinct.
"Understanding the rise and fall of Homo erectus highlights that humanity isn't, and never has been, immune to the impacts of climate change."
